description: Asymmetric $q$-Gaussian Distributions from Tsallis Maximum Entropy. Within the framework of non-extensive statistical mechanics, $q$-Gaussian distributions arise as maximum-entropy solutions of Tsallis entropy under suitable escort moment constraints. Although widely used in physics, biology, geology, finance, and related fields, standard $q$-Gaussians are intrinsically symmetric and cannot capture asymmetric fluctuations often observed in empirical data. We ask whether asymmetry can arise from the Tsallis maximum-entropy principle without externally skewing or joining distributions. We show that this is achieved by retaining the Tsallis entropy and imposing a global escort mean together with distinct downside and upside escort semi-variances. The key step is to reformulate the problem of maximum Tsallis entropy in terms of the escort density. The nonlinear escort constraints then become affine, while maximizing Tsallis entropy becomes equivalent to maximizing a strictly concave functional over a convex feasible set. Consequently, any admissible stationary solution is the unique global maximizer of the corresponding variational problem. The finite-sample approximation properties of the proposed asymmetric $q$-Gaussian are studied through Monte Carlo experiments using synthetic data generated from Azzalini skew-Student distributions. Compared with the classical symmetric $q$-Gaussian, the asymmetric specification systematically provides a closer approximation to synthetic asymmetric heavy-tailed distributions. Finally, we fit the model to return series from major equity indices, a commodity, and cryptocurrencies, and compare its in-sample goodness of fit with that of a symmetric $q$-Gaussian. The results show that the asymmetric model offers a closer in-sample description of unconditional return distributions, most clearly in the tails.
label: q-fin.ST

description: GROMM: Generative Risk-neutral Option Market Models. We present a statically and dynamically arbitrage-free European option market model with smooth interpolation between option prices, based on the SANOS framework, and prove that its dynamics admit a unique strong solution. In spirit, it is a stochastic model for local volatility when the latter is used as a representation of a European option price surface, not as a pricing model. We illustrate the strength of our approach on S&P Index Option data from January 2022 to August 2025. We show that the model's initial state fits within bid/ask for more than 95% of relevant market option prices. We then train the model dynamics under $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ and show that the model is indeed free of arbitrage while fitting the dynamics of the market well. We also propose a range of BHW-tests to test for absence of arbitrage.
label: q-fin.MF

description: The Buffett Effect. We study whether stock disclosures by recognizable investors generate abnormal market reactions beyond the reactions produced by comparable but non-recognizable managers. We define the Buffett effect as the incremental abnormal return to a disclosed new position that is attributable to the public recognition of the disclosing investor. We construct a recognition index from Wikipedia pageviews and ProQuest news mentions. Using data from 2000 to 2025 we compare market reaction to disclosures of 24 recognizable discretionary funds with disclosures of 24 matched control funds. New-position disclosures by recognizable managers generate a positive disclosure premium over the filing date and the following trading days, and the premium increases with investor recognition. We construct calendar-time portfolios that mechanically copy each group's disclosed purchases and find that copying the most recognized investors earns a significant alpha that persists for months and does not reverse. The evidence is most consistent with an entangled attention-information channel: investor recognition directs scarce investor attention toward selected disclosures, and the information revealed in those disclosures is then capitalized into prices.
label: q-fin.ST

description: Structured SDEs for Realized GARCH: Continuous-Time Volatility Modelling and Component-Level Analysis. We propose a structured continuous-time stochastic volatility model for one-day-ahead integrated-variance forecasting. The model introduces a jointly evolving realized-measure state that feeds directly into latent variance dynamics, while correlated Brownian innovations capture return-linked dependence. Parameters are estimated through simulation-based predictive learning, and Monte Carlo simulation forecasts integrated variance. Across 17 equity indices, the proposed model shows strong out-of-sample performance relative to GARCH, GARCH-Itô, Realized GARCH, HAR, and HEAVY benchmarks under QLIKE, MSE, and MAE. Ablation results show that realized-measure feedback provides substantial incremental forecasting value within the proposed framework, while return-linked Brownian dependence contributes more modest complementary gains. The results support incorporating measurement-driven information directly into continuous-time latent volatility dynamics to improve integrated-variance forecasting.
label: q-fin.ST

description: Portfolio Decarbonization under Incomplete Carbon and Transition Information. We study dynamic portfolio decarbonization under incomplete information about firms' carbon intensities and the underlying transition state. The investor maximizes expected utility of terminal wealth net of a penalty on perceived cumulative financed emissions. Asset returns and carbon intensities depend on a stochastic transition factor, while the investor may need to infer the current transition state, its long-run mean and firms' carbon intensities from market observations and periodic noisy disclosures. The optimal strategy combines a Merton-type component with climate-dependent expected-return adjustments, a direct carbon intensity penalty and intertemporal hedging demands associated with stochastic carbon intensities and learning. In a numerical application, incomplete information has limited effects on welfare and target satisfaction when prior beliefs are well specified. By contrast, biased beliefs generate welfare losses in either direction but asymmetric environmental consequences: optimistic and pessimistic beliefs induce opposite portfolio tilts and therefore affect the probability of exceeding the cumulative emissions target differently.
label: q-fin.MF

description: Risk Measures for the Climate Transition Age: Why Symmetric Risk Budgets are unlikely to mitigate two-dimensionally asymmetric Climate Change risks. The most widely used investment risk measures - variance, standard deviation, and tracking error - treat upside deviations as equally undesirable as downside losses. In stable markets with assumed symmetric return distributions, this simplification is potentially harmless. In the climate transition age, it is not. Climate risk is two-dimensionally asymmetric, across assets and over time. Both dimensions are negatively skewed against investors. Hence, climate transition investment strategies deliberately deviate from benchmarks that reflect an insufficiently decarbonising global economy. When fiduciaries enforce tracking error budgets that penalise outperformance just as heavily as underperformance, they inadvertently constrain exactly the portfolio return opportunities that climate-aware investing seeks. We argue that replacing symmetric deviation-based risk measures with their downside-only counterparts - semi-variance, standard risk and trailing error - resolves this conflict without sacrificing any fiduciary discipline. The distinction is not merely semantic: as the gap between climate transition trajectories and market benchmarks widens over the coming decades, symmetric risk budgets will become binding constraints on transition strategies well before actual investment risk warrants it. We propose specific changes to mandate design that would allow institutional investors to pursue climate transition opportunities within genuinely risk-aware (rather than deviation-averse) frameworks.
label: q-fin.RM

description: The Missile and the Toll: Two-Way Flow Through the Strait of Hormuz. Tolls for safe passage and attacks on shipping are usually treated as mutually exclusive: either ships pay or attacks happen. We argue they are complementary. In a Stackelberg escalation game for the Strait of Hormuz, the enforcer chooses an attack intensity and a toll schedule; the response is to pay, cross exposed, wait, reroute, or exit. Attacks create the willingness to pay; tolls harvest it. The model predicts asymmetry across trade forms: a toll where the cargo owner can pay and the vessel owner will consent, and none where either fails. Any such payment is clandestine, but the model's implications are testable against freight rates, insurance premia, and incident reports.
label: q-fin.PM

description: Common Signals, Spurious Cross-Excitation, and Identification in Multivariate Hawkes Processes. Multivariate Hawkes models are widely used to measure endogenous interactions in event data, but latent common signals can generate apparent excitation even without structural interaction. We characterize the resulting linear projection and construct stable, nonnegative Hawkes processes that share the mean intensity and Bartlett spectrum of common-signal models despite having different excitation mechanisms. This establishes a concrete form of second-order non-identification. We derive integrated third-order cumulants for Hawkes processes with Cox immigration and establish generic local identification of normalized structural parameters in two- and three-dimensional systems. An exact-equivalence Monte Carlo experiment demonstrates how third-order information can distinguish mechanisms with identical second-order structure, while revealing substantial finite-sample limitations under weak signals. For a restricted parametric family, we develop Whittle estimation from binned counts, establish consistency and asymptotic normality under appropriate identification conditions, and construct feasible sandwich standard errors accounting for estimated mean intensities. Simulations assess structural recovery and inference accuracy. An application to cryptocurrency transactions illustrates the sensitivity of inferred excitation to model specification and the limitations of structural interpretation based on spectral fit alone.
label: stat.ME

description: Data-Driven Dynamic Portfolio Selection with Vine Copula Simulation and Reinforcement Learning. We develop a data-driven approach to dynamic portfolio selection that combines vine-copula simulation with reinforcement learning. The investor has constant relative risk aversion and maximises expected terminal utility with a running penalty on the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of one-period losses. We estimate a conditional vine model from historical returns and use it to generate joint scenarios for CVaR evaluation and conditional paths for training a recurrent portfolio policy. Under uniform local derivative bounds, we propagate edgewise pair-copula parameter errors through the conditional transforms to obtain power-law stability bounds in Hellinger distance and total variation. In a finite-horizon investment model, we combine these estimates with a marginal and structural approximation budget to bound policy values, optimal values and the true-market loss of policies selected under a fitted model, with separate simulation and numerical optimisation terms. On a seven-asset panel comprising US and Chinese equities and gold, the selected ensemble of ten trained policies achieves a compound annual growth rate of 34.13% and a Sharpe ratio of 2.31 over 22 complete monthly holding periods, exceeding the corresponding values of six classical and vine-based benchmarks. Combining simulated and historical training data reduces monthly target-to-target turnover by 41.5% relative to training on historical data alone, while maintaining comparable growth.
label: q-fin.PM

description: Regime Detection in Latent Factor Models -- A Bayesian Decision-Theoretic Approach. Regime-switching multi-factor models are widely used in quantitative finance, but filtering does not by itself determine when an agent should act on inferred regime changes. We formulate online regime detection with latent factors and hidden regimes as a Bayesian decision problem balancing false alarms, detection delay, and misclassification. Since posterior regime probabilities are generally non-Markovian, the problem is represented as a measure-valued optimal stopping problem and approximated using particle filtering with Monte Carlo dynamic programming. A single-change-point Heston model provides a benchmark. With observed variance, the problem reduces to a two-dimensional Markov free-boundary problem, while under latent variance decisions are based on the filtered posterior measure. Numerical experiments in Heston and regime-switching Vasicek models show that the latent-information procedure can outperform feasible plug-in rules.
label: q-fin.MF

description: Loss-versus-rebalancing with external proportional transaction costs. We study liquidity provision in automated market makers when trading in the external market incurs proportional transaction costs. We consider both separately collected fees and fees retained in reserves. The benchmark is a self-financing strategy holding the same total risky inventory and trading at the external bid and ask. Under continuous external prices and pure arbitrage, the pool and benchmark have identical liquidation wealth whenever the pool fee or the external spread is positive. Thus loss-versus-rebalancing relative to this transaction-cost benchmark is zero, even without a pool fee if the external spread is positive. We then construct retained-fee utility-indifference pools that implement admissible decreasing inventory schedules, and geometric mean pools that implement feasible constant no-trade boundaries for portfolio weights. These results offer an investment interpretation of liquidity provision: by choosing the pool design, a liquidity provider can specify a trading strategy whose rebalancing is carried out by arbitrageurs.
label: q-fin.MF

description: Where Backtests and Live Trading Part Ways: Six Defects from One Intraday System. Backtests of intraday strategies can drift away from what the live system actually does; in our case, the drift never showed in summary statistics. We report six defects found while running one intraday US equity system live and comparing its live days with their backtest replay. Three came from data: a default feed that carried a small fraction of real opening volume, historical prices adjusted for dividends that live orders never see, and data the live system downloaded but the backtest never did. Two came from code: a sizing step that exceeded a limit the live account enforces, and UTC timestamps read as New York time. One came from configuration: settings that were switched on but never reached the code that places orders. For each we give the symptom, the size of the error, the cause and the test or control that now guards against it. All six sat where two paths that should agree had drifted apart. We close with a ten-point checklist. We make no claim about whether the system is profitable.
label: q-fin.ST

description: Reading the News Without Hindsight: NoLBERT Topics and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns. Language models that read financial news are usually trained on text from the same years used to test them, so a backtest can reward hindsight. We build news topics from NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, adapted into a sentence encoder by contrastive fine-tuning on passages of the same article, with no labels or returns. We compare it with LDA, MiniLM and FinBERT readers on 1.26 million articles from 2012 to 2024, convert each reader's topics into attention shocks and stock exposures, and forecast the returns of the 1,000 largest US stocks with eight models at three rebalancing frequencies. Models are fitted on 2013-2019, choices are made on 2020-2021, and 2022-2024 is held out. The experiment with the best validation score loses money at every frequency. Measuring attention shocks against the past 63 trading days instead of 5 raises the test rank IC of every reader. NoLBERT gives the most stable topics and forecasts about as well as LDA. An equal-weight combination of all readers and models earns a monthly net Sharpe ratio of 1.12, significant against zero before adjusting for the search but not against a price-only benchmark.
label: q-fin.ST

description: Market Efficiency in a Changing Asset Population: Mobility, Entry, and Survival over Cryptocurrency's Full History. Weak-form efficiency implies symmetry restrictions on the Markov chain governing movement across the cryptocurrency capitalisation distribution. We test them on the full listed population: 8,970 assets, 690 weekly cross-sections, 2013 to 2026, with entry, exit and survival observed rather than inferred. Symmetry is rejected in every era, but the asymmetry falls by seventy percent, and what converged is entry-driven compositional churn rather than coins' own valuations. The bottom decile earns 27.5% per week on paper and nothing among assets that trade, on capacity of $293,000. Compensation for neglect exists precisely where trading does not.
label: q-fin.ST

description: Multiplayer games on regular graphs under aspiration-driven imitation: Fixation probabilities and the dilution principle. We investigate how cooperation evolves in multiplayer games on regular graphs of degree $k$ when individuals base their decisions on both their own aspiration levels and the success of their neighbors. We calculate explicit first-order formulas for fixation probabilities using pair approximation and diffusion methods under weak selection. These formulas separate aspiration effects from payoff effects filtered by the graph. We show that increasing the graph degree attenuates the selection effects driven by payoffs. In contrast, the contribution of the aspiration gap $Δα=α_D-α_C$ is independent of graph degree at first order. We apply the framework to public goods, stag-hunt, and snowdrift games and obtain corresponding conditions for the evolutionary success of cooperation. In the public goods and stag-hunt games, the conditions at large degree retain cost terms, so cooperation requires a sufficiently positive aspiration gap to compensate for the cost of contributing. In the snowdrift game, both benefit and cost contributions vanish in the locally tree-like regime at large degree, leaving the aspiration gap as the leading first-order contribution. Monte Carlo simulations on connected random regular graphs of degree $k$ are consistent with the first-order predictions within their formal regime of validity, while simulations outside this regime are interpreted only as qualitative checks of the predicted trends.
label: q-bio.PE

description: Heterogeneity among and competition between life stages together extend the stability boundary of complex ecological communities. Classical models of pairwise species interactions consistently predict that large, complex communities are inherently unstable, yet the observed persistence of diverse communities highlights a central contradiction in theoretical ecology. While foundational frameworks often model species as homogeneous populations, one theoretical resolution lies in including internal species structure. In this work, we incorporate explicit demographic stage structure into a generalized Lotka-Volterra framework to evaluate how ontogenetic changes throughout the life cycle of a species can affect whole-community stability. We show that stage-dependence of inter-specific interactions can significantly expand the stable parameter space for a species network. Furthermore, this enhanced stability requires strong competition between life stages of a species. Our study illustrates that stage structure with population heterogeneity expands classical stability criteria, providing a mathematical foundation for understanding how ontogeny modifies the classically derived complexity boundaries for local asymptotic stability.
label: q-bio.PE

description: From Alpha to Execution: Trading Horizons, Regimes, and Schedules under Concave Impact and Hurst Scaling. Classical execution models assume linear impact, diffusive prices, and an exogenous horizon. We study execution under concave power-law impact and Hurst-scaled price fluctuations, and make two contributions. First, we choose the execution horizon by maximizing the Sharpe ratio of the trade's realized P&L. Price moves during the execution window are part of that P&L, so executing more slowly reduces its variance, and because impact is concave it can also lower cost per share. Urgency comes only from alpha realized while the order is being worked. The problem is governed by the signs of two quantities: (i) the duration elasticity of impact $a$, which under a structural prior equals the impact-persistence gap $β- H$ and can take either sign; and (ii) the net urgency $ν$, the rate of alpha realization net of exposure relief. When $ν$ keeps its sign over the window, an interior optimum exists, to leading order in $T/t_f$, only when both are positive; otherwise the order should be worked at the fastest or slowest admissible pace. In the interior regime the first-order condition involves no impact coefficient, order size or volume, and the objective is flat: for a large-cap example, the window within 1% of maximal Sharpe spans more than an order of magnitude. Second, given the window, we derive the schedule shape by convex programming under an envelope cost. For any increasing per-share cost of delay $w(t)$, the KKT solution is $φ\propto (λ- w(t))_+^{1/β}$. For a Hurst-scaled envelope $w \propto t^H$, the normalized schedule depends only on $(β, H)$, has a closed form via the incomplete beta function, is front-loaded, and tapers smoothly to zero, saving 10-17% of envelope cost relative to a constant-rate (TWAP) schedule of equal duration. Whether it uses the whole window depends on a single dimensionless robustness level, for which we give a calibration.
label: q-fin.TR

description: Microbial Methanogenesis on Mars: A Life Detection Target for an MLE-Type Mission and Future Human Exploration. Methane (CH4) is one of the most enigmatic and potentially consequential trace gases detected on Mars, having demonstrated apparent seasonality, localized plumes, or, depending on who you ask, never conclusively detected at all. While the Martian methane mystery remains unsolved, it has sparked a vibrant area of astrobiology research exploring whether microbial methanogenesis -- one of the simplest and most ancient metabolic pathways -- could plausibly proceed under various extreme physicochemical conditions characteristic of the Martian shallow subsurface. The emerging consensus is a cautious but compelling "possibly". These findings elevate methanogenesis as both a top priority candidate biosignature for extant life detection and a justification for urgently advancing in situ instrumentation capable of definitively detecting CH4 and constraining its origin, biotic or otherwise
label: astro-ph.IM

description: Rachev-Ratio Portfolio Optimization with TimeGAN Scenarios: Replacement versus Supplementation. This study evaluates the reliability and investment consequences of scenarios from a specified time-series generative adversarial network (TimeGAN) in Rachev-ratio portfolio allocation. Using 12 exchange-traded funds, we compare historical, replacement and hybrid policies across five training seeds with delayed execution and transaction costs. Synthetic probability mass varies independently of draw count under a fixed training protocol; optimal generator fidelity is not assumed. Generated scenarios understate volatility and tail losses and distort dependence. Limited longer-training diagnostics improve reconstruction loss without improving cross-asset correlation accuracy. Higher-mass hybrids earn larger average net returns in some configurations, but all conditional generated-versus-historical return intervals include zero at the reference block length. Full-period TimeGAN means exceed resampling controls, while direct paired return, Sharpe and realized-tail-ratio intervals include zero. Replacement raises turnover and is sensitive to the modified objective's denominator floor; changing that floor does not uniformly improve realized downside risk. Exploratory generation-error associations do not identify a causal investment-performance channel. The results illustrate financial model risk from the interaction of imperfect scenarios and a tail-sensitive allocation criterion, supporting joint evaluation of fidelity, numerical behavior and realized outcomes within the tested implementation.
label: q-fin.PM

description: Optimal Trading Filters and the Value of Predictive Signals. The value of a forecast depends on its accuracy, but also on its actionability. In trading, an investor must translate return forecasts into positions while accounting for trading costs and the lingering impact of earlier trades. We solve the stationary quadratic trading problem with transient price impact using tools from prediction theory: Wiener-Hopf factorization gives the optimal policy as the composition of a conditional forecast and an explicit causal linear filter. We recover the Gârleanu-Pedersen aim-portfolio under exponential resilience and derive fractional trading filters under power-law impact decay, requiring memory beyond finite-dimensional LQR control. At fixed positive risk penalty, signals of equal instantaneous predictive strength have equal frictionless Markowitz value. With trading costs, net attainable value is determined by the mean square of the friction-weighted conditional forecast. Under power-law impact with exposure bleeding, we find an intermediate optimal mean-reversion rate for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck signals.
label: q-fin.MF

description: More Mentions, Less Information? Diagnosing Identity and Alignment in Reddit Embeddings for Volatility Forecasting. Since the 2021 GameStop short squeeze, r/WallStreetBets (WSB) has been associated with episodes of extreme volatility, and its text is increasingly used to forecast volatility. A model using only large language model (LLM) embeddings of WSB posts attains an out-of-sample $R^2$ of 0.13 for log realized variance. That number shows predictive power, but it does not reveal where the information comes from or how much the text adds beyond a firm's own volatility history. We answer these questions with a diagnostic protocol that nests embeddings on a heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) benchmark, compares them with text-free firm-identity controls, shuffles the day-to-text pairing within firm-years to test day-specific alignment, and checks whether gains persist across periods and coverage groups. We apply the protocol to frozen LLM embeddings in a panel of 202,145 mentioned stock-days, using retrospective rolling out-of-sample tests over 2015-2022. The results indicate that most of the standalone fit reflects firm or firm-year information: on firms seen in training, a text-free firm baseline reaches $R^2 = 0.32$, shuffling preserves 89-92% of the standalone fit, and masking ticker strings reduces standalone $R^2$ to -0.005. Adding embeddings to HAR reduces equal-date MSE by 1.22% (95% CI [0.94, 1.49]). This small but statistically significant gain survives firm controls and ticker masking, but is largely eliminated by alignment shuffling. The gain is concentrated in 2015-2019 and is not distinguishable from zero in 2020-2022. Expanding coverage by 48% through off-hours and weekend posts adds stock-days with no reliable positive increment. More mentions therefore do not imply more incremental forecasting information.
label: q-fin.ST

description: Compiling Environment Classifiers to Contextual Modal Types. Type systems for metaprogramming take one of two approaches to safeguarding the scopes of variables in generated code. They either use Environment Classifiers (EC) to identify scopes by name (Taha and Nielsen, 2003), or they use Contextual Modal Type Theory (CMTT) to match scopes by structure (Nanevski, Pfenning, and Pientka, 2008). In this paper, we connect these two approaches by compiling a calculus with polymorphic environment classifiers, subtyping, and mutable references to a CMTT-based calculus with polymorphic contexts, mutable references, and first-class substitutions. The key idea is to map each environment classifier to a context. We prove that the compilation preserves types and that compilation preserves the behavior of metaprograms. Both proofs are mechanized in Agda. The compilation shows that CMTT is at least as expressive as environment classifiers. We conjecture that the converse compilation is difficult, because environment classifiers impose a stricter regime on the metaprogram.
label: cs.PL

description: Amortized Neural Filtering for Calibrated Posteriors in Statistical Arbitrage. Statistical arbitrage trades on an estimate of the state of a residual spread, and conventional practice discards the uncertainty of that estimate. We keep the uncertainty and use it in the trading decision. A Neural Filter Estimator (NFE) is trained on simulated paths of a mean-reverting process whose innovation law is selected by testing candidates against real residuals; once trained, it returns the posterior over the latent state of every spread in a cross-section in one forward pass. Three results follow. On simulated paths with known truth, every practical estimator, ours included, falls in one narrow band of accuracy well below an estimator given full information, so the posterior gains no accuracy over a point estimate; its contribution is a correct account of its own uncertainty. On Korean equities, net of costs, the conventional point estimate forecasts about a thousand basis points per holding period more than it realizes, and the amortized methods cut that gap by a factor of roughly two to eight. Sizing positions from the posterior on the same learned factors as the end-to-end Attention Factor Model matches the Sharpe ratio of those factors under the base rule within the period's noise, at no more risk.
label: q-fin.GN

description: Conflicting History in Foundation Model Return Forecasts. Older observations can help a forecaster learn a predictive relationship while becoming misleading when that relationship changes. We study this tension using paired return histories that differ in older observations but share recent returns and the conditional distribution of the next return. Across five foundation-model forecasting procedures and three simulated processes, each evaluated on 1,024 independent replications, conflicting history reduces the probability of improving on zero in all 30 higher-signal comparisons. This loss of usefulness occurs despite successful signal recovery under stable conditions. A separate exploratory comparison on 56 assets finds that shortening inputs from 256 to 64 returns increases mean absolute error for every model by 1.77-4.58 basis points; neither length improves observed overall error over zero. The evidence distinguishes the ability to extract a signal from the ability to withstand conflicting history, while showing why context sensitivity alone does not justify discarding older data.
label: q-fin.ST

description: HP-GSBS: Accelerating greedy state boundary search with reusable interval statistics. Greedy State Boundary Search (GSBS) identifies transitions between relatively stable neural activity patterns, but repeated candidate evaluation makes large analyses expensive. HP-GSBS is an open-source Python package that reorganizes the search around reusable interval contributions and correlation statistics. Streaming candidate reduction and local refinement further reduce repeated work; CPU, PyTorch CUDA and Triton backends share sequential segmentation decisions. Across seven controlled workloads with two realizations each, median same-input speedups range from 154 to 1730 times. All 168 optimized executions reproduce original boundaries and selected state counts, with maximum absolute t-distance difference $1.88\times10^{-11}$. Four frozen EEG recordings provide complementary validation, including a complete input-to-segmentation application example. Batch processing, versioned result persistence and optional low-memory execution support recording collections and longer inputs. By removing redundant computation, HP-GSBS makes established neural-state segmentation faster while preserving its scientific outputs.
label: cs.CE

description: Blame-aware Recomposition for Secure Compilation Proofs of Low-Level Compartment Isolation. The security guarantees of existing formally verified compilers for compartmentalized programs in unsafe languages like C stop at a rather high level, assuming a built-in protection mechanism and a block-based memory model. Verifying a concrete, low-level enforcement mechanism for compartment isolation is still a major challenge for current proof techniques. In particular, Abate et al.'s proof technique fails because one of their proof steps, recomposition, essentially requires hiding all information about the code of each compartment, which is not practically achievable at a low level. We propose an extension of their proof technique to a low-level setting where compartments can fully observe each other's code. To do so, we introduce an overlay semantics that allows us to characterize these observations as a form of undefined behaviour, and we use a novel variant of recomposition that we call blame-aware recomposition, which essentially allows recomposing executions as needed in the original high-level proof technique, even if the low-level context observes the code, because this context is ultimately going to be discarded. We apply this new proof to a compartment isolation mechanism that uses a programmable tag-based reference monitor.
label: cs.PL

description: Distributions of metric $n$-point invariants and applications to molecular evolution. Datasets often arise as samples from a metric measure space whose geometry reflects the data-generating process. We introduce metric $n$-point invariants, defined as functions of the pairwise distances of $n$-point configurations, to study the geometry of such spaces. This provides a unified framework for existing concepts, such as the pairwise distance itself, the Gromov product, and Vietoris-Rips persistence diagrams. The distribution of a metric $n$-point invariant $F$ over random $n$-point configurations can be used to extract geometric information from the space and is obtained as the pushforward of Gromov's $n$-th curvature measure $μ_n$ along $F$. Our main result is an explicit bound for the expected $p$-Wasserstein distance between $μ_n$ and the empirical curvature measure $\hatμ_{n}$ of finitely many sampled $n$-point configurations, and carries over to the associated distributions of Lipschitz metric $n$-point invariants. From this we derive the sample size needed to achieve a prescribed accuracy and level of confidence in the approximation of the curvature measure. As an application, we use metric $n$-point invariants to study molecular evolution. We describe how site-wise nucleotide frequencies shape the corresponding distributions in Jukes-Cantor and Halpern-Bruno substitution models, and analyse five million SARS-CoV-2 genomes, revealing increasingly common failures of the four-point condition, constrained nucleotide accessibility consistent with the biased mutation spectrum, and rare cycles in persistent homology reflecting recurrent mutations across lineages. These findings demonstrate the potential of our sampling-based approach to the geometry of data as a scalable, phylogeny-free tool for detecting and quantifying evolutionary structure in large genomic datasets.
label: math.MG

description: Higher-Order Co-Infection on Hypergraphs. People encounter infections through overlapping groups, such as households, classrooms, and workplaces. Understanding how these shared contacts affect the spread of multiple pathogens is critical to determining what information epidemic models need to retain. We introduce HyCo-SIS (Higher-order Co-infection SIS), a discrete-time SIS model on hypergraphs with explicit reinforcement between overlapping active groups and pairwise transmission. We investigate how this reinforcement affects infection dynamics and whether simplified representations of hypergraphs preserve the resulting behavior. We derive an exact representation of overlap reinforcement as target-dependent four-person interactions and determine when a symmetric representation is possible. Numerical experiments examine reinforcement strength, contact structure, and susceptibility to secondary infection, as well as calibrated pairwise approximations. Our results demonstrate that redistributing overlap weights can substantially change finite-time co-infection even when every individual's total overlap coefficient is preserved. We further derive an exact five-person calculation and demonstrate why equal mean infection pressure does not necessarily produce equal acquisition probabilities. These findings identify how the allocation of higher-order interactions can influence contagion dynamics beyond their aggregate strength. Beyond epidemiology, this work contributes to the statistical physics of spreading processes by examining how the arrangement of many-body interactions shapes collective dynamics, and what information is lost when those interactions are simplified.
label: physics.soc-ph

description: Demonstration of continuous non-invasive monitoring of plant metabolism using mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy. Life is a rhythmic process driven by cellular and physiological mechanisms that allow plants to respond and adapt to their environment. In addition to natural fluctuations, plants are increasingly exposed to environmental stresses, mainly caused by climate change and anthropogenic pollution. Multiple approaches across different biological scales (gene, cell, metabolite, and physiology) have shed light on acclimation mechanisms but generally lack sufficient temporal resolution. Establishing a non-invasive and high-temporal-resolution monitoring method to measure plant activity across different conditions is therefore needed to fully assess how plant metabolism changes under stress. Here, we established a novel approach to perform continuous and non-invasive mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy on vascular plants, with the aim of identifying and monitoring the chemical composition of peripheral tissues, including sap, over periods ranging from a few minutes to several months. We describe an experimental setup, the physics underlying its operation, and present a multi-day acquisition. Compared with controls, data enabled to identify a diurnal pattern, with peaks of approximately equal duration, that recurred consistently over the experiment. Estimations of the impact of instrumental and environmental fluctuations indicate that the signal amplitude and trends cannot be explained by instrumental drifts. The experiment thus demonstrated the detection of a signal associated with plant physiological activity. While its origins remain to be clarified, this preliminary experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the measurements and provides a basis for future developments.
label: physics.ins-det

description: The resource cost of cooperative invasion. A contact network can favor cooperation by sheltering a lineage until its descendants compete with defectors as a group. We determine the contact strengths, invasion times and measurement effort needed to realize this advantage at fixed population size. Individuals reproduce according to averaged cooperation payoffs, and offspring replace neighbors through contacts of equal weight in both directions. Contact contrast is the ratio of strongest to weakest contact. Under weak selection on a six-site path, the least contrast needed to favor a single cooperator over the reverse invasion by a defector grows as $656ε^{-2}$ for uniformly placed mutants and $4050ε^{-3}$ for mutations in newborn offspring, as the benefit-cost ratio $b/c=1+ε$ approaches one. The extra power arises because rare replacement protects a site while suppressing mutation arrival there. Global bounds force two weakly coupled groups and exact mirror symmetry of the least-contrast contacts for sufficiently small $ε$. Under uniform introduction, additional contrast shortens the leading mean time to extinction or fixation in the absence of selection, from $12/ε$ toward $6/ε$ reproduction attempts, and eventually breaks the mirror symmetry of the fastest design. Estimating the uniform-introduction advantage from fixation outcomes of independent completed invasions defines a third optimum. Within the six-site family with mirror-symmetric, strongly separated contacts, we optimize contacts and selection strength with reproduction weighted linearly or exponentially by payoff. At fixed relative precision, with contrast a fixed factor above its minimum, the leading summed trial duration grows as $ε^{-3}$. Efficient measurement accepts a smaller advantage in exchange for shorter trials. The cheapest, fastest and most efficiently measured networks therefore differ.
label: q-bio.PE

description: Polarized Scheme: duality of computation, delimited control, and continuation-passing macro Interleaving. Static type systems for Scheme have traditionally followed one of two paths: manifest type checking with multi-dispatch (Clifton and Leavens, 2005) or latent occurrence typing tailored for untyped interoperation (Tobin-Hochstadt and Felleisen, 2008). In this paper, we propose Polarized Scheme, a static foundation built upon polarized type theory and the duality of computation. In Polarized Scheme, values are positive data producers (A+) and continuations are negative observation consumers (~A+). Functions operate symmetrically under dual viewpoints: as forward value-transformers and as backward continuation-transformers. Computation exists exclusively at the interaction cut executed on a focus-and-context abstract machine separating positive data focus from negative return contexts (R). Delimited control (shift/reset) and continuation marks are expressed directly as Return Stack frame operations parameterized by the prompt's ambient answer type without polluting producer data types. Furthermore, we formalize the hygienic macro system as an interleaved continuation-passing pipeline, where macro expansion erects its own continuation hierarchy nesting into runtime evaluation. We prove Subject Reduction, Progress with respect to prompt-delimited stacks, prove Duality Bisimilarity, characterize Return Stack reclamation for dynamic closures, and report on an executable reference implementation in a verified dialect of Go with a verified cut-elimination dispatcher
label: cs.PL

description: PyGPLA: A Python Package for Generalized Phase Locking Analysis. Spike-field couplings measure the links between neuronal spiking and local field potential (LFP) and provide a tool to study how neural populations coordinate activity across spatial and temporal scales. While modern high-density electrophysiology enables the simultaneous recording of numerous LFP channels and neuronal units, this massive scale poses significant statistical and computational challenges for conventional pairwise coupling analyses. The number of channel-unit comparisons grows rapidly, and a coherent population-level structure can be obscured by high-dimensional coupling matrices. Generalized Phase Locking Analysis (GPLA) addresses this challenge by organizing spike-triggered LFP phase information into a complex coupling matrix and extracting dominant low-rank modes. These modes summarize whether a population is coupled to the field, which channels and units contribute to the coupling, and how their relative phases are organized. Here, we present PyGPLA, an open-source Python package implementing GPLA for high-density electrophysiological recordings. Designed for straightforward integration into existing neural data analysis pipelines, PyGPLA supports multivariate spike-LFP coupling analysis, from coupling estimation and interpretation to significance assessment using analytical and surrogate-based tests.
label: q-bio.NC

description: Affective Valence as the Interoceptive Rate of Change of Jacobian Scale. Affect is widely held to depend on interoception. This paper proposes that valence is the rate at which interoception moves a self-sustaining system's responsiveness relative to its terminal set (roughly, death). Responsiveness is formalised as the scale of the system's Jacobian and interoception as its internal inputs: receptors, signals and forecasts of its energy reserve. Changes in responsiveness that bypass interoception, such as brain damage, are not felt. Language models have no valence because they are not self-sustaining. The chain rule splits valence over the system's parts and the causes that affect its internal inputs. With the log scale, these splits account for need-dependent pleasure, diffuse hunger and localised pain, negativity bias, and relief when a threat fails to arrive. In a minimal model of a body: (1) Blocking the reserve signal leaves depletion unfelt, and driving it produces hunger with an undepleted reserve. (2) Removing receptors or their gain, or driving receptors, reproduces congenital insensitivity to pain, asymbolia and phantom pain. (3) A receptor gain learned to sustain the body signals local damage to the whole body, so an injury hurts in proportion to its cost. (4) If the reserve also modulates the gain, the body learns to suppress pain due to receptors as energy runs low. (5) When it learns to maximise its own scale, it becomes a wirehead. The account explains when changes are felt, where they are felt, and when feelings mislead.
label: q-bio.NC

description: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks. Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.
label: q-bio.QM

description: Online Preplay and Offline Replay Optimize Action Selection in a Closed-Loop Navigation Model. Hippocampal neurons not only encode the animal's current position, but also generate sequences representing potential future states and past locations. During goal-directed navigation, the represented location sweeps ahead of the animal's location (online forward replay). After such tasks, during rest, neuronal sequences occurring during sharp-wave ripples replay previously explored trajectories (offline forward replay). Following random foraging, however, neuronal sequences resemble Brownian motion, which does not correlate with behavior (diffusive replay). The mechanisms producing such diverse sequences, and their distinct effects on spatial coding and navigation, remain unclear. Here, we address these questions using a closed-loop model of navigation in a two-dimensional open-field environment based on a spiking neuronal network. In our framework, neuronal sequences are generated by a common mechanism driven by background noise and the balance of excitation and inhibition. Different replay modes arise solely from task-dependent synaptic modifications and serve different functions: online forward replay facilitates shortcut discovery, offline forward replay consolidates optimal sequences of actions, and diffusive replay helps in generalizing the action and state map and homogenizing internal connectivity. Together, these results show that a single network architecture can flexibly generate various replay types and clarify how each contributes to optimizing goal-directed navigation behavior.
label: physics.bio-ph

description: Regime-Aware Interpretable Ranking for Sector Rotation. Sector rotation is a common decision in benchmark-relative portfolio management, where portfolio managers rank sectors for overweight and underweight positions. We formulate this task as ranking sector actions by expected future risk-adjusted active performance, measured with forward sector-benchmark Sharpe ratios. Such rankings should preserve temporal information, express model outputs through economically familiar signal characteristics, account for changes in signal relevance across macroeconomic environments, and capture dependencies among sectors. We propose RegimeRank, an interpretable sector-ranking model that represents fundamental and technical signals through expert-defined temporal characteristics, conditions them on learned macro factors via cross-attention, and models cross-sector dependencies through self-attention. Expected-gradient attributions identify the contributions of individual signal-transformation pairs, while macroeconomic and cross-sector attention maps provide diagnostics of the learned conditioning and relational structure. We evaluate RegimeRank on weekly S&P 500 data from 2002 to 2024 under combinatorial purged cross-validation, where it outperforms representative ranking and machine-learning baselines across multiple ranking metrics. Ablation studies support the contributions of latent macro states, regime conditioning, and cross-sector modelling, while attribution and attention analyses illustrate the temporal characteristics, macro states, and sector relationships underlying its rankings.
label: q-fin.PM

description: A Type System for Communication-Safe Hardware Design. Hardware components communicate through clock-cycle-sensitive protocols. Hardware Description Languages (HDLs), however, provide limited support for expressing these protocols or for checking that independently developed components agree on them. When components disagree, the composed design can perform unsynchronized exchanges or stop making progress. We call these failures communication-safety violations. Communication safety is therefore a global property, determined by interactions between multiple components. This makes it difficult to check modularly. This paper presents Pact, a typed extension of Anvil for modular verification of communication safety in synchronous hardware. Pact types describe message-passing, control-flow, and clock-cycle behaviour. Each component is checked against its type. Compatible types then guarantee that the components compose into a communication-safe system. Pact also supports incremental design. It can check a subsystem before the full system context is available. The check produces a summary type that captures the communication behaviour left for future compositions. To reduce annotation burden, Pact infers types by abstracting payload values while preserving communication, timing, control, and fairness. These inferred types are optimal for the checker: whenever some checker-accepted types can prove compatibility, the inferred types can prove it as well. Type inference and type checking are decidable, and compatibility is decided by a sound and complete algorithm. We implement Pact by extending the Anvil compiler and evaluate it along four dimensions: detecting communication errors during incremental design, expressiveness on ten clock-cycle-accurate translations of open-source hardware IPs, compatibility-checking time, and generated hardware overhead. Pact expresses realistic protocols and verifies all ten benchmarks in reasonable time.
label: cs.PL

description: Probability-Weighting Functions for Normal Tempered-Stable Laws: Orthogonal Channels and Information-Theoretic Indices. A probability-weighting function (PWF) maps objective probabilities into decision weights. We construct PWFs from changes in the distribution of returns rather than from a parametric family: with prior and posterior return distributions $F_{prior}$ and $F_{post}$, the PWF is $w(p) = F_{post}(F_{prior}^{-1}(p))$. Both distributions are normal tempered-stable (NTS), and the posterior differs from the prior along one of three channels, each isolated with the variance held fixed: scale, skewness and tail thickness. Around a symmetric benchmark with excess kurtosis 3, a 40% change in scale moves cumulative probabilities by up to 7 to 8 percentage points, a skewness of $\pm 0.5$ by 2 percentage points, and a change of $\pm 0.3$ in the tail index by about 2 percentage points. The three channels leave distinct signatures: the deviation $w(p) - p$ changes sign once, twice and three times, respectively. Three information-theoretic indices (a Fisher-normalized logit shift, a signed Jensen-Shannon divergence and a log-odds elasticity) summarize the distortions and avoid the endpoint singularity of the classical ratio $(w(p)-p)/[p(1-p)]$. Applied to NTS parameters calibrated to S&P 500 ETF daily returns over 2015-2025, the same channels produce distortions of 2 to 7 percentage points. Code that reproduces every figure and number in the paper is provided.
label: q-fin.MF

description: Rational T cell repertoire allocation to control the gut microbiota. The gut microbiota shapes host metabolism, development and immunity, yet how the host regulates its composition in the presence of complex ecological interactions remains poorly understood. Recent experiments that measured T cell reactivity to individual strains in germ-free mice inoculated with a defined microbial community found that T cell recognition across microbial strains is sparse but broad, with a few polyspecific clones recognizing antigens shared across taxonomically diverse strains. Reanalyzing these experiments, we show that these T cell responses are associated with abundance changes of the strains they target. To interpret these findings, we develop a model linking the T cell repertoire to microbial abundances, in which a repertoire is allocated to minimize microbe-driven harm at the cost of maintaining an immune response. The model rationalizes the observed sparsity of gut T cell reactivity and shows that this allocation can emerge from competition between T cells for microbe-derived antigens. Finally, we find that while immune recognition can regulate microbial abundances, ecological interactions between strains may interfere with this mechanism. Together, these results provide a quantitative framework for immune control of gut microbial composition and identify principles governing the organization of T cell repertoires in the gut.
label: physics.bio-ph

description: SARP: An On-SSD Index for KVCache with Fast Prefix Matching and Recovery. Distributed LLM serving relies on a global index to locate reusable key-value cache (KVCache) blocks through prefix matching. Losing the index after a crash or restart forces affected requests to recompute existing KVCache on GPUs. Persisting the index restores access after a failure. Existing persistent indexes face a tension between prefix-matching performance and recovery time. A snapshot-backed in-memory index supports fast prefix matching, but rebuilding the full index delays recovery. An on-SSD index avoids this rebuild, but adds storage accesses to prefix matching. Our core insight is that extending a matched prefix over a short span typically requires distinguishing only a few token sequences, suggesting that sparse in-memory routing state may suffice. Prefix matching also accesses block metadata in sequence order, allowing metadata for consecutive blocks to be retrieved together. We present SARP (Sparse Adaptive Routing and Packing), an on-SSD KVCache index for fast recovery and prefix matching. SARP groups consecutive block IDs and metadata into segments to amortize storage accesses across multiple blocks. A compact in-memory routing directory identifies candidate segments using entries at selected block positions. SARP limits segment retrievals and uses compact filters to prioritize candidates with longer potential matches. After retrieval, SARP verifies block IDs against the query and reuses only KVCache blocks covered by the verified prefix. After a restart, SARP restores the sparse routing directory from a snapshot. Across four multi-turn chat and agentic workloads, SARP recovers 8.0x to 77.5x faster than the in-memory index baselines and delivers 1.15x to 66.6x the request throughput of the on-SSD index baselines, while reusing only 0.0030% to 0.029% fewer tokens than exact prefix matching.
label: cs.DB

description: Dynamic portfolio selection under range value-at-risk with logarithmic returns. This paper studies continuous-time portfolio selection under Range Value-at-Risk (RVaR), with both portfolio performance and risk evaluated in terms of logarithmic returns. We formulate a mean--RVaR problem in a continuous-time financial market and reduce the dynamic optimization to a static quantile problem. Using quantile representation, Lagrangian optimization, and convexification, we characterize the optimal terminal wealth through the convex envelope of an RVaR-specific transformed weighting function. The RVaR-specific convex envelope exhibits two distinct geometric configurations. Under Scenario~1, the terminal wealth has a VaR-type structure: the minimum-RVaR payoff is digital-option-like, whereas for $0 0$, pure minimum-RVaR optimization may assign zero terminal wealth in sufficiently bad states because the extreme quantile region $[0,α)$ is excluded from the RVaR criterion. These results clarify how interval-based quantile risk control shapes state-dependent portfolio payoffs and connects RVaR with its VaR and ES limiting cases.
label: q-fin.RM

description: Anchored Exploration in Product Evolution: A Phylogenetic Network Framework for Semiconductor Designs. We develop a product phylogenetic network framework for examining anchored exploration. Using 102,465 semiconductor products grouped into 45,996 design families, we distinguish accumulated design continuity (Anchor) from externally precedented feature additions (horizontal transfer, HT). Fitted regressions yield non-monotonic relationships for HT occurrence and descendant carriage, alongside increasing within-family carriage over observed support. These patterns connect technological trajectories and recombination by distinguishing the continuity associated with incorporating external features from that associated with reproducing them in subsequent products.
label: physics.soc-ph

description: Cross-disorder Learning of Imaging-derived Joint Mophometric Markers in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Diseases. As two most prevalent neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) shared commonalities both in symptomology and pathophysiology. However, to what extent and in what way these two distinct disorders overlap remain underexplored. In this study, we propose an explicit, interpretable and spatially adaptive transfer learning framework to elucidate the morphometric biomarkers linked to AD and PD. We applied such high-dimensional machine learning model to two most popular open-source neuroimaging datasets, i.e., Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). On the one hand, our cross-disorder classifier revealed neuro-anatomical alteration patterns well aligning with previous neuroimaging research findings and underscoring patients' clinical presentations. On the other hand, the spatially adaptive trained classifier using shared prior achieved statistically superior diagnostic performance compared to respective individual models, which further highlights the cross-disorder framework's efficacy on modeling limited-size datasets across disease domains.
label: q-bio.QM

description: Caterpillar trees are asymmetric, balanced trees are symmetric. Two conjectures of Allman, Long and Rhodes are proven. The ultrametric exchangeable model captures the symmetries in allele distributions of ultrametric mechanistic models of coalescence and substitution in mathematical phylogeny. The dimension of this model with respect to the species tree leaf count is shown to be greatest for caterpillar trees and least for balanced trees.
label: q-bio.PE

description: Does a Flux-Defined Markov Blanket Screen Self-Replicating Gray--Scott Spots? A Computational Test of a Blanket Condition from the Free Energy Principle. Friston's free energy principle holds that a system separated from its environment by a Markov blanket---a boundary whose states statistically screen its interior from its exterior---can be treated as performing approximate Bayesian inference, and that such blankets arise wherever coupling is short-range. We test this blanket condition in a concrete nonlinear pattern-forming system: self-replicating spots in a reaction-diffusion model that persist, compete, and reproduce. Directed boundary exchange and timescale separation hold up reasonably well, with qualifications. A flux-defined blanket does not screen interior from exterior. Flux removes only part of the linear dependence, and a nonlinear test shows that conditioning on flux \emph{increases} the dependence, consistent with conditioning on a collider, since flux is a joint function of concentrations on both sides of the boundary. The dependence is concentrated within about one organism radius of the boundary. A band of the surrounding field that thick screens the interior from the exterior beyond it, as any short-range field would, which is not evidence of inference.
label: q-bio.NC

description: Is sophistication a panacea? The learning capacity of random feature models for financial forecasting. This paper investigates the ability of random feature models to learn more complex patterns than the simple negative autocorrelation of financial returns. Theoretical insights highlight that the learning capacity of random features ridge regression is determined by the interplay between signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) level and regularization. We characterize the different learning regimes through the derivation of a particular threshold: the SNR frontier. Practically, our results permit to determine the minimum penalty level to be introduced into the estimation process in order to guard against a drop in the SNR during the implementation phase. We empirically apply this methodology to equity premium forecasting and use the output to build mean-variance efficient portfolios. The resulting portfolios yield substantial economic value over a portfolio construction scheme based on a short-term reversal strategy.
label: econ.EM

description: SweepANN: A GPU-Accelerated Large-K Approximate Vector Search for Drug Discovery. DrugCLIP places small molecules and protein pockets in one space, turning genome-wide drug discovery into large-K retrieval by vector proximity. A campaign fixes over 20K pockets in advance for one library of over 500M molecules. Each pocket keeps K = 500K candidates, 0.1% of the collection, versus 100 in ANN benchmarks. Missed hits never get tested, so mean recall must reach 99% relative to exact search. Large answers make IVF probe every list holding a result and graph search track K or more candidates, so costs grow with K. On our CPUs and GPUs, neither index family reaches the target without losing most of its edge over scanning. SweepANN partitions compressed vectors across GPUs and scans each resident partition. One matrix multiplication scores each block for a whole query batch, reading it once. Several plans perform the K-dependent selection and merging of each query's K answers, each returning an exact top-K under compressed scoring. The window plan retains each query's best K from sampled blocks as its seed, and only rows above each seed's minimum score, shared once across GPUs, enter the buffers. Four Blackwell GPUs (RTX PRO 6000) answer all 26,562 pockets with a resident time of about 61 seconds, excluding library loading, and 99.6% mean recall relative to exact FP32 search. DrugCLIP reports roughly 24 hours with eight A100 GPUs in its own campaign. On 500M rows, the window plan runs 1.41x faster than SweepANN's grouped plan in the same memory. Across 25M-500M rows and K of 10K-500K, all GPU IVF configurations meeting the recall target take 8.2-24x SweepANN's resident time. On DEEP1B's 1B vectors across eight GPUs, against SweepANN's exact full-score scan of uncompressed FP32 rows, the window plan cuts resident time by 5.4x and 3.2x at K = 100K and 500K. It also cuts per-GPU peak memory by 6.0x and 5.3x, losing 1.0 and 0.7 mean-recall points.
label: cs.DB

description: Discrete Choice with Generalized Social Interactions. This paper studies social interactions in discrete choice models in which individuals can respond differently to different network members, conforming to some while distinguishing from others. In this generalized framework, I show how to use within-network variation in individual choices to draw inference about differences in endogenous interaction effects, while accounting for unobserved contextual effects. I also show how to construct internal instruments to correct for measurement error bias, a key source of endogeneity in network models with incomplete information. I apply these results to data from two empirical settings: classroom peer effects in Tennessee primary schools and spillovers in deworming treatment uptake in Kenya. In both applications, I find that differences in social interaction effects, with individuals conforming more strongly to similar peers, play a key role in shaping people's choices, with implications for the targeting of policy interventions.
label: econ.EM

description: Multifractality of human upper-limb velocity tracks motor optimization via hand dominance experiment. Theoretical goal-directed movements follow a unique, stereotyped velocity profile, but continuous movement has no unique optimal solution, so it is unclear whether motor optimization makes continuous movement more stereotyped or more diverse. Previous studies indicated higher information content in the dominant hand, suggesting greater diversity. Because continuous velocity is a composition of overlapping joints movement of varying form, timing and amplitude, comparable to the events that compose spike trains and heartbeat series, we asked whether this diversity appears as a wider multifractal spectrum of velocity. We applied multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis to motion-capture velocity of cursive handwriting from right- and left-handed participants writing with both hands; hand dominance is a natural experiment in which task and geometry are fixed while optimization varies. With the dominant hand, spectra were wider, had a lower dominant exponent and were more positively asymmetric in both groups, whereas hands with the same functional role did not differ between groups. A logistic regression on the three spectral features identified the dominant hand with a cross-validated AUC of up to 0.93. Optimized continuous movement is thus not more stereotyped but more diverse: complex, neither stereotyped nor random, with multifractality that tracks hand dominance.
label: nlin.AO

description: Evidence-Based Policy Choice in Macroeconomics. This paper studies data-driven macroeconomic policy choice in a structural VAR framework. We formulate the policymaker's problem of optimizing the future path of a policy instrument as a statistical decision problem under two alternative policy regimes: a "contemporaneous" regime, where the chosen path is implemented through unexpected policy shocks each period, and a "forward guidance" regime, where the expected path is announced in advance and enforced through anticipated policy shocks. We derive oracle, Bayes-optimal, and robust Bayes decision rules, the last for the case where structural impulse responses are only set-identified, and show that the decision problem depends on the structural rotation matrix only through the span of the columns associated with the policy shocks. We argue that the plug-in rule is uniformly dominated by a James-Stein-type shrinkage rule in a local asymptotic Gaussian limit experiment, and is therefore inadmissible therein. Numerical analysis calibrated to monetary SVARs compares the risks of the plug-in and a benchmark Bayes rule in Monte Carlo Gaussian simulations and finds that the Bayes rule attains lower risk at 95.1-99.9 percent of the posterior draws in the two regimes. We then study the relationship between the one-shot decision for a policy path and sequential policymaking, and show that, in the contemporaneous regime, the one-shot oracle path coincides with the expectation of the sequentially optimal oracle plan; we document that this representativeness property fails under Bayesian decision-making with parameter uncertainty. In an application to U.S. monetary policy in 2006-2007, we find that the plug-in and Bayes rules can differ substantially: the Bayes-optimal rule prescribes an initial tightening followed by partial easing across different specifications, while the plug-in changes across regimes.
label: econ.EM

description: Collective-Variable Stein Variational Gradient Descent for Free Energy Surface Exploration. Enhanced-sampling methods enable molecular simulations to access configurational regions that are difficult to explore with conventional dynamics, but their efficiency often deteriorates as the number of collective variables (CVs) increases. Here, we introduce an enhanced-sampling framework that couples Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) with parallel restrained molecular dynamics simulations to facilitate exploration of higher-dimensional CV spaces. SVGD collectively transports an ensemble of interacting particles toward a target probability distribution by combining mean forces that guide particles toward low-free-energy regions with kernel-mediated repulsive interactions that maintain particle diversity. We validate the approach using an analytically solvable double-well model, followed by aqueous alanine dipeptide and tripeptide in two- and four-dimensional CV spaces, respectively. In each case, the particle ensemble reproduces the corresponding target distribution, and the reconstructed free-energy surfaces agree closely with analytical or umbrella-sampling references. For alanine dipeptide and tripeptide, CV-SVGD requires substantially less aggregate MD sampling than the corresponding umbrella-sampling reference calculations. These results demonstrate the potential of CV-SVGD as a flexible, parallelizable framework for enhanced sampling in multidimensional CV spaces. We additionally provide an open-source Python implementation to facilitate its adoption.
label: physics.bio-ph

description: KatoANN: Enabling Near-Exact Vector Search at the Speed of Lossy Scans with CPU Matrix Engines. Distance scans in partition-family approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search are typically limited by memory bandwidth. Existing systems therefore improve throughput by reading fewer bytes per candidate, often at the cost of recall. We present KatoANN, a CPU ANN search system that removes this tradeoff by batching distance scans on Intel AMX, a CPU matrix engine. Batching allows multiple queries to reuse each fetched vector code, shifting the scan from memory-bound to compute-bound and enabling near-exact distances at the speed of a lossy scan. KatoANN stores each vector once as a 16-bit SQ16 code split into high- and low-byte planes. Its adaptive rank-then-refine scan first ranks all candidates using only the high byte, then refines a small survivor set using the full-byte code. Both stages use the same representation, avoiding a second copy of the raw vectors. Experiments across diverse high-dimensional workloads show that KatoANN is the fastest partition-family ANN search system in our evaluation throughout the high-recall range.
label: cs.DB

description: Record Types Everywhere. This paper introduces a novel calculus that models first-class environments and function application paradigms using standard record types. By proposing new extensions to general record types, we achieve a design that is remarkably simple and principled. We formalise this design in a core calculus and prove several desirable properties, including type soundness, normalization, and a simulation of the simply typed lambda calculus. Additionally, we extend the design with mutable references. The calculus, its semantics, along with the extension, and all stated properties are fully mechanized in the Lean 4 proof assistant, alongside an interpreter formally verified to be equivalent to the operational semantics.
label: cs.PL

description: TriGeoBench: A Multimodal Mathematical Geometry Benchmark with Figures and TikZ. Multimodal Large Language Models show strong vision-language capabilities, yet their geometry-centric reasoning remains insufficiently understood. Existing mathematical benchmarks typically rely on rasterized figures and cover limited geometric knowledge areas and response formats, making it difficult to assess whether models reason over geometric structures or exploit superficial visual patterns. We introduce TriGeoBench, a geometry-centric multimodal benchmark constructed from Chinese middle- and high-school mathematics examinations. TriGeoBench contains 7,000 question-answer pairs and 12,235 geometric figures with TikZ code, spanning plane geometry, solid geometry, analytic geometry, function, and vector geometry across diverse response formats. Each instance forms a {question-answer pair, image, TikZ} triplet: question-answer pairs are stored in LaTeX, images as RGB figures, and TikZ preserves geometric topology, symbolic annotations, and relational structure. We evaluate representative open- and closed-source MLLMs through image-to-TikZ and multimodal reasoning probes. Results reveal persistent fine-grained structure and image-text alignment challenges. Oracle experiments with human-curated reference TikZ suggest that accurate executable representations provide complementary geometric cues; they do not evaluate an end-to-end conversion pipeline. TriGeoBench offers a testbed for structure-aware mathematical reasoning.
label: cs.AI

description: Market Regime-Based Multi-Asset Portfolio Optimization Using Nested Clustered Optimization for Tactical Asset Allocation. We propose a regime-aware tactical asset allocation (TAA) framework integrating market regime detection with Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) for multi-asset portfolio construction. The central hypothesis is that incorporating market regime information into the NCO pipeline, specifically at the stages of covariance estimation, hierarchical clustering, and weight optimization, yields portfolios with improved risk-adjusted performance and reduced downside risk relative to regime-agnostic baselines. Market regimes (Bullish, Sideways/Neutral, Bearish) are detected using a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) fitted exclusively on information available up to each decision point, thereby preventing look-ahead bias. Regime-conditional covariance matrices and clustering structures parameterize NCO at each rebalancing event. An adaptive rebalancing rule, triggered by regime transitions or material changes in optimal weights, replaces fixed-calendar rebalancing. The framework is evaluated on a heterogeneous monthly multi-asset universe comprising Indonesian government bonds (SBN), the LQ45 equity index, gold (IDR-denominated), foreign exchange (CNY/IDR), and Bitcoin/IDR (BTC). Out-of-sample performance is assessed via rolling walk-forward backtesting. Benchmarks include equal-weight (1/N), buy-and-hold, standard NCO without regime awareness, minimum variance, hierarchical risk parity (HRP), and a rule-based regime strategy. Performance metrics include cumulative return, annualized Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, maximum drawdown, Calmar ratio, turnover, and net-of-cost returns. Statistical significance is assessed using the Jobson-Korkie test. The empirical analysis indicates that the proposed regime-aware TAA framework successfully limits tail risk, achieving a maximum drawdown of 4.44% and demonstrating the utility of HMM-based regime detection in multi-asset risk management.
label: q-fin.PM

description: Central Limit Theorems for Optimal Transport Functionals. We establish central limit theorems for empirical plug-in estimators of scalar functionals of quadratic optimal transport maps and potentials, including Wasserstein costs and several risk measures constructed from transport-based multivariate quantiles. We study the one-sample problem with a known reference distribution and i.i.d. observations from the target distribution. A natural approach is to combine a limit theorem for the empirical transport map with the functional delta method. We show, however, that in dimensions at least two, empirical transport-map errors admit no nonzero weak limit in $L^2$ under any normalizing scale. Instead, we linearize the functional directly in the target distribution, obtaining an influence-function expansion with a remainder controlled by the transport-map error. The influence function is characterized by a linear elliptic partial differential equation. Under regularity conditions, we use this expansion to prove central limit theorems in low dimensions and establish validity of the empirical bootstrap. We also derive semiparametric efficiency bounds and show that the plug-in estimators attain them under the same conditions.
label: math.ST

description: Containment of Conjunctive Queries with Negative Information over Semirings. We study the containment problem for (unions of) conjunctive queries ((U)CQs) with negative information on semiring-annotated databases. Our approach to negative information follows the treatment of negation proposed by Grädel and Tannen (2017, 2019, 2021 and 2024) for first-order logic and fixed point logic which applies productively to large classes of semirings, including bounded distributive lattices, as well as the important provenance semirings studied for positive CQ containment by Green (2009). Negation features in (U)CQs along two dimensions: negated equalities (disequations), and negated relational atoms. We study complexity for each of them separately, as well as jointly.
